Question: Is a defendant legally obligated to enter a plea of "guilty" or "not-guilty" in court? Can they choose not to answer and remain silent?
Answer: Sure they can stay silent, but in modern practice, if they do, the court will enter a “not guilty” verdict on their behalf. It’s not like the good old days where they would lie you on the floor and put stones on your chest until you entered a plea. That’s another thing ruined by the “woke mob”. But in the United States, you have four plea options: Not Guilty (prove it!) Guilty (I admit everything) No Contest (I’m not admitting anything, but you can punish me as if I did) Alford (I’m innocent, but there’s enough evidence to convict me right now and I can’t refute it)

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do we use Latin letters to write in English instead of using a different set of letters that are more closely related to the language's Germanic origins?
Answer: Early English, as has been noted, had it’s own alphabet, borrowed from the Norse. It was called Runic and was made to be easily carved with all straight lines. But as England became Christian, the most literate people you had were monks and priests, and they started doing all the royal paperwork. The priests and monks knew Latin, and were more familiar with that alphabet, so they adapted it to English - rather poorly as it turned out, but there you go. By the time of the Norman Conquest the Latin alphabet was widespread throughout Europe so it largely became the standard. English just followed suit and adapted it to their own needs, including about half-a-dozen English only letters that have since become obsolete.

Question: What is the purpose of canals or rivers in cities? Is it just for aesthetic purposes?
Answer: Until about 200 years ago, the only way to economically transport low value high volume goods, like grain, was over water. That’s why a lot of big cities either sit on a river, or are where a river meets a larger body of water like a lake or an ocean. For example Tokyo Delhi and Shanghai The three largest metro areas on the planet are all next to a river. Other major cities on or near a river are London (on), Paris (on), New York (near), and even St. Petersburg (more on that later). Navigable rivers allow you to trade all the way to where the river meets falls or rapids, which explains why Montreal is where it is The Lachine Rapids drop about 30 feet from Lac de Deux Montagnes to the Port of Montreal, which means ships can’t use that channel. Back in the 1840s, you can see what they built to get around them, the Lachine Canal. The Lachine uses a series of locks to raise boats to the lake, after which there are more locks on both the St. Lawrence River and the Ottawa River allowing barge type vessels to take goods to Ottawa, Toronto and beyond. But in 1959, they built an even better canal for larger ships which is still in commercial use, the St. Lawrence Seaway. That and two other canals allow ships to get all the way to Minnesota. The St. Lawrence Seaway through Montreal, on the far right and bottom of the picture - longer and wider than the Lachine, it can carry ocean going ships. Because controlling a river is so important to trade, many river deltas have been completely changed to ensure control over the waterway. To allow the water to continue to flow through, several channels are dug that serve double duty as drainage and transportation corridors. For example: St. Petersburg Amsterdam Now, railroads made lots of canals obsolete. Railroads don’t require a constant flow of water, and it’s easier to run a rail line over a gorge than a canal, although it is possible. The Pontcysyllte Aqueduct in Wales finished in 1805. Now only used for recreational purposes. 38m above the River Dee, it’s the highest navigable aqueduct in the world. But lots of canals have fallen into disuse, like these ones in Quebec that were replaced by the St. Lawrence Seaway Old lock on the Soulange Canal, north of the St. Lawrence River. The Newmarket Canal, obsolete while it was being built in the late 19th century. But for a lot of cities, the river is their lifeblood - their reason for being. The Detroit River, as it goes by Detroit (right) and Windsor, Ontario (left). The river allowed the raw materials for car manufacturing to be easily shipped to automobile factories, and allowed the finished product to be shipped by sea as well.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the difference in pronunciation between "th" and "f" in English? Is the pronunciation of these letters the same in French, even though they may be written differently?
Answer: English has two sounds that are represented by the letters “TH”. Both of them are “dental fricatives” because the tongue has to extend past the teeth to make the sounds. The first is the sound in a word like “the”. It’s made by holding the tip of the tongue against the front of the top row of teeth. The second is the sound in a word like “thin”. It’s made by holding the tip of the tongue just through the teeth. The /f/ sound is made quite differently, by holding the teeth over the lower lip. The tongue remains entirely within the mouth. Most languages, including most European languages and even all the Germanic languages, don’t have dental fricatives. That means if you’re not an English speaker, you’re not used to moving your teeth, lips and tongue in that manner to make the sound. It’s quite a difficult sound to make and most English speakers don’t master it until they’re around five years old - that’s fairly late for a language sound that’s very common in English. In Germanic languages, the words that take a dental fricative usually use a /t/ sound instead (e.g. “thousand” versus “tausend”). The /t/ sound is made by holding your tongue at the back of your top teeth where they meet the roof of the mouth, entirely different. When trying to pronounce dental fricatives, most Germanic languages just substitute a /t/. Dental fricatives don’t exist in French either, and most French speakers also make substitutions. If you’re from France, you tend to substitute a /z/ sound, which is made by holding your tongue just behind your closed teeth. “The” and “thin” become “ze” and “zin”. If you’re French Canadian, you tend to substitute a /d/ sound, which is made similar to a /t/ sound by holding your tongue slightly farther back. “The” and “thin” become “de” and “din”.

Question: If you were in charge of renaming Canada’s national animal, what would you pick and why?"
Answer: The common name of our industrious, indefatigable, furry national animal is the “Beaver”. It appears that pretty much every language in Europe used a similar word for this animal, which several hundred years ago was widespread throughout that continent until we got a taste for wearing hats made out of its pelt and hunted them to near extinction. Luckily, it recovered and there are about 1.2 million European beavers at the moment. However, although Canadian beavers and European beavers are the same genus, they’re different species. Their genus name “Castor” comes from the Latin word for “wood”. The European species is “Castor fibre” as “fibre” is the Latin for the animal (and it’s a cognate of “beaver”, from the same root). Here in North America, they’re “Castor canadensis” or “Canadian wood”. They’re much more common here, and estimates are that there are about 15 million of them. Beavers are often treated as a nuisance, but they help with old growth forests (they prefer younger, faster growing, more tender trees, leaving older trees room to grow) and it turns out their dam building prevents things like loss of soil and wetlands. One farmer who let beavers have the run of his property found that even during dry times, his crops never lacked for water. So maybe they need a more majestic name. Luckily, the beaver is well known to the First Nations. There are, of course, many indigenous names for the animal, but I’m going with Algonquin for this one as they did a lot of trading. So our new name will of course be “Amik”, which is what they called it.
